rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to retain weakly retained compounds while eluting strongly retained compounds, with ample final hold time. The retention and resolution pattern will guide subsequent gradient and temperature optimization.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing whether the current resolution margin accommodates faster elution. Keep starting composition and temperature fixed to isolate the effect of gradient steepness.
Keep the fast gradient and test temperature-driven selectivity changes in the crowded middle peaks. Raising temperature may improve their separation while preserving the zero time penalty.

Increase temperature by a smaller step to further separate the remaining critical pair while monitoring the narrowing gap between peaks 4 and 5. Retain the fast gradient to preserve the zero time penalty.

Test the low-temperature selectivity regime, since warming improved one critical separation but created another. Keeping the gradient fixed will reveal whether cooling produces a better-separated elution order without a substantial time penalty.

Test a steeper gradient at 50 C to shift selectivity in the remaining critical pair while retaining more separation between peaks 4 and 5 than at 55 C. The shorter gradient should preserve the zero time penalty.

A modestly shallower gradient should improve the critical separation at 55 C while retaining the temperature-driven separation of the other middle pair. The last peak is expected near 7.7 minutes, potentially preserving the zero time penalty.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to test a neighboring method around the maximum-scoring condition. This may improve the earlier critical separation while keeping the last peak near 8 minutes and preserving adequate separation of the later critical pair.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a higher starting organic fraction to assess a neighboring condition with potentially faster elution. Monitor both critical middle-pair separations to determine whether the maximum score is preserved.

Slightly flatten the gradient to improve the critical separation from injection 9 while retaining its improved separation of the other middle pair. This condition may achieve the maximum CRF with more balanced resolution margins and a last-peak time below 8 minutes.

Reduce the endpoint another grid step to bring the remaining critical resolution above 1.5 while retaining adequate separation of the other middle pair. The last peak is predicted near 8 minutes, making this a candidate for the maximum CRF with more balanced resolution margins.

Use a gradient slope between injections 10 and 11 to target both critical resolutions above 1.5 with the last peak slightly below 8 minutes. This may preserve the maximum CRF with more balanced resolution and time margins.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step from injection 12 to shorten retention and potentially improve the later critical separation. The earlier critical pair has some resolution margin, so this tests whether the maximum CRF can be retained with better-balanced separations.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test a faster, high-temperature selectivity regime. This combination may move the troublesome middle compounds past an elution-order crossover and restore separation at substantially shorter retention times.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction widens the middle-pair separation after the apparent elution-order crossover at 60 C. This explores a faster alternative to the maximum-scoring methods, while checking for loss of early-peak resolution.

This gradient slope lies between injections 10 and 11, targeting both critical resolutions above 1.5 while keeping the last peak below 8 minutes. The lower endpoint should still elute all compounds because it exceeds the outlet organic fraction at their observed elution times.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test the temperature sensitivity of the maximum-scoring method from injection 12. This isolates a 5 C increase and checks whether its critical separations remain acceptable.

Test the lower-temperature neighbor of injection 12 to complete the temperature-sensitivity assessment. The maximum CRF is already achieved, but this run will establish whether cooling preserves separation or makes the later middle pair critical again.

Lengthen injection 13’s gradient to improve its limiting separation while retaining the stronger resolution of the later middle pair. This tests whether a higher starting organic fraction can provide larger resolution margins without a significant time penalty.

Slightly flatten injection 19’s gradient to raise its limiting resolution above 1.5 while preserving the later pair’s stronger separation. The last peak should remain near 9 minutes, testing another potentially maximum-scoring condition with improved resolution margins.

Preserve injection 7’s starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while ending the gradient earlier at a lower organic fraction. Since all peaks previously eluted before this gradient would end at the outlet, the maximum CRF should be retained.

Keep the successful gradient slope but begin the final hold before the last peak elutes. This tests whether a lower endpoint preserves the maximum CRF while leaving the critical middle separations unchanged.

Preserve injection 11’s gradient slope and temperature while lowering the endpoint to 0.60. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, retaining its maximum CRF and slightly larger minimum-resolution margin than injection 7.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 11 to assess the width of the maximum-score region. The earlier critical separation should improve, while the later pair is expected to remain above 1.5 and the last peak near 8.5 minutes.

Use the final injection to test another implementation of the maximum-scoring gradient slope from injection 7. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, preserving CRF 1.000 and the 7.60-minute last-peak time.
